summary: Describes extensions that can be added to TLS, with a generic mechanism for extending the client and server hello messages and specific extensions that use it. It is a proposed standard and was replaced by RFC 4366.

eli5.summary: TLS is the way computers secretly talk. This memo adds a way for them to mention extra options when they say hello.

subtitle: Extensible mechanisms for TLS handshake messages and six specific extensions for constrained clients.

tldr.problem: TLS was designed for traditional wired networks but is increasingly deployed on wireless and constrained networks with bandwidth, memory and power limitations. Basic TLS does not allow clients to specify which server they are connecting to, does not support smaller message sizes or OCSP status responses embedded in the handshake.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3546 provides a generic extension mechanism that lets clients and servers negotiate new features via hello extensions. It defines six specific extensions: Server Name Indication (SNI) for virtual hosting, maximum fragment length negotiation for constrained clients, client certificate URLs for memory efficiency, trusted CA indication to avoid handshake failures, truncated HMAC to reduce bandwidth, and certificate status request for OCSP.
tldr.outcome: TLS can now adapt to constrained environments while remaining backwards compatible with TLS 1.0 servers that do not support extensions. The Server Name Indication extension became widely adopted for HTTPS virtual hosting.

today: RFC 3546 was obsoleted by RFC 4366, which clarified and expanded the extensions. The Server Name Indication (SNI) extension became foundational for modern HTTPS, enabling secure virtual hosting. Many of the other extensions remain in use today, particularly on mobile and IoT devices facing memory or bandwidth constraints.

sections.title: The Problem of Extending TLS
sections.content:
TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the cryptographic protocol that secures HTTPS and many other Internet applications. When TLS 1.0 was designed, it was optimized for traditional wired networks with abundant bandwidth and computational power. However, TLS is now deployed on constrained devices like mobile phones, wireless access points and embedded systems that have limited memory, bandwidth or battery life. These environments create new requirements that the original TLS design did not address.

RFC 3546 solves this problem by introducing a generic extension mechanism into the TLS handshake. The mechanism allows clients and servers to negotiate new features using extensions in the client hello and server hello messages. Six specific extensions address the most critical needs of constrained devices, and future extensions can be added using the same mechanism. The mechanism is designed to be backwards compatible: TLS 1.0 clients and servers that do not understand extensions can still communicate with those that do.
sections.eli5: TLS is used everywhere now, including on devices that have limited memory or battery. This RFC adds a way to ask for features that help with these constraints, and it does it in a way that old software can still talk to new software.

sections.title: Extension Architecture
sections.content:
The extension mechanism works by adding a new field to the TLS client hello and server hello messages. A client hello can now include an extension list containing zero or more extensions. Each extension has a type (identifying what feature it represents) and extension data (specific to that type). The server responds with extensions of its own, indicating which ones it supports.

The format is simple and extensible: each extension is identified by a numeric type and contains opaque extension data. Six extension types are defined: server_name (0), max_fragment_length (1), client_certificate_url (2), trusted_ca_keys (3), truncated_hmac (4), and status_request (5). The standard is designed to ensure that servers never send an extension type in a server hello unless the client requested it first, preventing compatibility issues.
sections.eli5: When a TLS client connects, it sends a hello message saying what extensions it supports. The server looks at that and responds with its own hello message saying which extensions it will use. This way they negotiate what features to use.

sections.title: Six Specific Extensions
sections.content:
Server Name Indication (SNI) lets a client tell the server which hostname it is trying to reach. This is crucial for virtual hosting, where a single server address hosts multiple domains. When the client sends its certificate selection or cipher suite decision, the server can use the SNI to choose the right certificate for that domain.

Maximum Fragment Length Negotiation lets constrained clients request smaller TLS record sizes (down to 512 bytes) instead of the standard 16KB. This conserves memory.

Client Certificate URLs allow clients to send a URL pointing to their certificate instead of sending the certificate data itself, saving memory on the client side. The server retrieves the certificate from the URL.

Trusted CA Indication lets clients tell servers which CA root certificates they possess. Servers can then choose certificate chains that the client can validate, avoiding handshake failures on devices with limited CA storage.

Truncated HMAC reduces the authentication tag size from the normal 160 bits (for SHA-1) down to 80 bits, saving bandwidth on constrained networks.

Certificate Status Request lets clients ask the server to include certificate status information (such as an OCSP response) in the handshake, avoiding the need to fetch CRLs separately and saving bandwidth.
sections.eli5: The first extension lets the client say which server it thinks it is talking to. The others save memory or bandwidth: smaller messages, certificates by reference instead of by value, knowing which CAs the client has, shorter authentication tags, and getting certificate status in the handshake.

sections.title: Security Analysis
sections.content:
RFC 3546 includes detailed security analysis for each extension. The server name indication extension does not introduce significant security problems as long as server administrators are aware that multiple domains share one address. The maximum fragment length and truncated HMAC extensions do not reduce security because TLS already supported fragmentation and because the truncated MAC (80 bits) remains secure given TLS's session-per-failure property.

The client certificate URL extension has more security concerns because the server must act as an HTTP client to fetch the certificate, potentially being manipulated to attack other hosts. Administrators should only enable this extension explicitly and configure only the URL schemes needed. The trusted CA indication extension could reveal which CAs a client trusts, a potential privacy concern. The certificate status request is generally safe because clients can still contact OCSP directly if needed.
sections.eli5: Each extension was checked for security problems. Most are safe. The certificate URL extension needs careful configuration because it makes the server fetch things from URLs. The CA indication might leak privacy information about which CAs you trust.

sections.title: Backwards Compatibility
sections.content:
A primary design goal is backwards compatibility. TLS 1.0 servers are required by the specification to accept extended client hello messages (they just ignore unknown fields). Extended server hello messages are only sent in response to extended client hello messages, preventing them from breaking old TLS 1.0 clients that do not expect them.

Furthermore, for most extensions, no mandatory server response is required when a client requests them. If a server does not support an extension, it simply does not include it in the server hello, and the client can proceed with normal TLS. This allows clients and servers to be upgraded independently without coordinating timing.
sections.eli5: Old TLS programs can talk to new TLS programs because the old ones just ignore the new extension types. The new extensions only activate if both sides agree on them.

sections.title: Error Alerts
sections.content:
RFC 3546 defines five new TLS alert types for extension-related errors. The unsupported_extension alert is sent by a client if it receives an unsupported extension in the server hello. The unrecognized_name alert is sent by a server if it does not recognize a server name in the SNI extension. The certificate_unobtainable alert indicates a server could not retrieve a certificate from a URL. The bad_certificate_status_response alert indicates an invalid OCSP response. The bad_certificate_hash_value alert indicates a certificate URL hash mismatch.

These new alerts are only sent after an extended hello has been exchanged, preserving compatibility with servers that do not understand extensions.
sections.eli5: When something goes wrong with an extension, TLS sends special error messages. These new error types only exist to explain problems specific to extensions.
